subsubtopic: AMNESTY INTERNATIONAL-"HUMAN RIGHTS NOW" CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week marks a major event for Amnesty International as it begins its "Human Rights Now" campaign here at home and around the world.
"Human Rights Now" heralds the fortieth anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as adopted by the United Nations and which defines the rights of humanity.
This campaign will strive to raise mankind's awareness and recognition of every individual's entitlement to human rights, and to encourage the Governments of the world to strengthen their domestic and international protection of human rights.
Today in Ottawa and across the country Amnesty International groups will be approaching Canadians to sign petitions promoting human rights which will then be circulated worldwide throughout the campaign. We as Canadians should applaud and support Amnesty International in its ongoing battle to protect our human rights and to improve the quality of life for people the world over.

subsubtopic: CANADA-ISRAEL FRIENDSHIP DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is Canada-Israel Friendship Day, a day that celebrates the friendship that has existed between Canada and Israel for the past 40 years. Since 1948 Canada has constantly supported Israel's right to exist as an independent state within recognized boundaries, and has played a leading role in peace-keeping and moderating in the Middle East.
This friendship has resulted in closer cultural and economic ties, including the establishment of a Joint Economic Committee on Trade and Economic Expansion, a Canada-Israel Cultural Foundation, and a Chair in Canadian Studies at Hebrew University. This special relationship with Israel has existed alongside and has been balanced by Canada's friendly relations with Arab nations in the Middle East.
Recently, Canadians have become more and more disturbed by the situation in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. I ask Israel as a long-time friend to use restraint in its dealings with Palestinians in the occupied territories. These violent actions aimed at crushing Palestinian unrest are contrary to the spirit and traditions of the Israeli nation.
Just as no lasting peace can be achieved without the recognition of Israel, there must also be recognition of the rights of the Palestinian people to a homeland. The animosity is real, and certainly presents a seemingly insurmountable obstacle to a lasting peace. But men and women of moderation must continue to work toward that goal. The Israel-Egypt agreement is a good example that the seemingly impossible can happen when historical enemies settle their disputes at a negotiating table.

subsubtopic: SYDNEY STEEL CORPORATION STRIKE-REFUSAL OF BENEFITS FOR OTHER LAID-OFF WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of this House the plight of the striking steel workers at the Sydney Steel Corporation. This House should know that because of the strike some workers have been laid off. Workers such as those in Locals 6516 and 6537 are not eligible for strike pay from the union because their locals are not on strike.
Two days ago the members in both locals were informed that the Unemployment Insurance Commission refuses to pay them their unemployment insurance benefits because they do not qualify under Section 44(1) of the Act. All of the players involved in this decision know that this is not a good enough reason to refuse benefits; it is a technicality. These men are not working due to circumstances beyond their control. They have families to care for and they need financial assistance while the strike continues.
I call upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to overrule this ridiculous decision and to release the unemployment insurance cheques to those needy workers. It is time for the Government of Canada to show some compassion and economic leadership and provide justice to those needy workers.

Petitions

subsubtopic: DESIGNATION REGARDING NORTHERN TAX ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a duly certified petition bearing a substantial number of signatures from the people of Dubreuilville, which is a small isolated community in northern Ontario. The petitioners know what it is to be underserviced. They have no bus service, no resident doctor or dentist, no bank, no lawyer or social workers.
They call upon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to broaden the regulations so that they may be included under the northern tax credit benefit program.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-OPPOSITION TO GATT RULING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a petition that was drawn up, certified, and signed today. It is from Canadian citizens who live in Prince Rupert, Surrey, Richmond, Vancouver, Powell River, Uclue-let, and in other places.
The petitioners point out that the preliminary GATT ruling has struck down Canadian export restrictions on unprocessed salmon and herring; that the majority of the West Coast fishing industry is opposed to the adoption of the ruling knowing that it would put the 4,000 jobs of B.C. shore workers in jeopardy.
The petitioners point out that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon), the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) have all failed to give assurances that they will do all in their power to stop the adoption of the GATT ruling. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has even refused to meet with members of the fishing industry lobby who are presently in Ottawa.
Today officials of the Department of External Affairs are proceeding to Washington to try to negotiate a bilateral agreement, but are unlikely to reach a satisfactory solution due to the U.S. intransigence.
Therefore, the undersigned citizens of Canada now avail themselves of their ancient and undoubted right to present the petition asking that Parliament fully support the West Coast fishing industry in its fight to stop the adoption of the GATT decision and take unilateral action to protect the jobs of Canadian workers, and retain our sovereign right to make decisions on allocating Canadian resources with the Government of Canada.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO TRANSPORT OF PLUTONIUM OVER NORTHERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and duty to present petitions signed by residents of communities in the Northwest Territories, namely, Lake
Harbour, Coral Harbour, Rankin Inlet, Cape Dorset, Sachs Harbour, and Fort Smith.
The petitioners are seriously concerned about the potential environmental results if plutonium is flown over Canada's north, as well as the potential contribution to nuclear proliferation.
The petitioners call upon the Parliament of Canada to recognize the dangers of such flights and say no to plutonium flights over northern Canadian territory.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 from a number of western Canadian constituents who believe that the Government does not have a mandate from the people of Canada by which to conclude a trade deal. The petitioners have many other concerns, Mr. Speaker, which you can read later. I will simply say that they are calling upon Parliament to dissolve to enable the people of Canada an opportunity to accept or reject the trade deal during a national general election.

ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN Ms. Marion Dewar (Hamilton Mountain) moved:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to make significant progress towards eliminating discrimination against women, especially in areas such as employment equity, child care, and programs for native women.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon to speak to the concerns of Canadian women. This is certainly a week when we celebrate the accomplishments of women. We must also recognize that many of the things that women have been fighting for over the years are not being realized.
Among the temporary special measures taken by the Government to eliminate discrimination against women is the adoption of employment equity legislation in June, 1986, legislation responding to the recommendations of Judge Rosalie Abella's landmark study on equality in employment. Judge Abella certainly did give us many recommendations that were worth while. Unfortunately, those recommendations were not taken into total consideration when the legislation was brought forward.
What does the legislation actually do? Does it truly respond to Judge Abella's recommendations? Does it work effectively to eliminate employment discrimination against women? The first major problem with the Act is that there is no real enforcement mechanism. Judge Abella had stated that, to be adequately enforced, the implementation of employment equity requires an independent agency to oversee the development of equity plans.
What does the legislation give us in terms of enforcement powers? First, it requires employers to file annual reports on the workplace composition, occupations, and salary ranges. While there is a penalty for not filing a report, it is too minimal to be of consequence for many of the large firms covered by the legislation, and could simply be absorbed by these firms as a business cost. There is no penalty, however, for failure to improve the workplace in terms of employment

March 9, 1988
Supply
equity. An employer could file the same report year after year and not be penalized for workplace discrimination.
Companies are also required to prepare action plans with goals and timetables to remove discriminatory practices. These action plans are held strictly confidential-don't let anybody know how we are discriminating, keep it a secret. There is no penalty for failing to develop an action plan. Employers are not required to file their action plans with the CEIC or with the Human Rights Commission, or even to post their plans in the workplace.
Employers are required to evaluate their "employment practices" and to institute "positive policies and practices" to achieve an equitable representation of target groups in the workplace. Neither "employment practices", nor "positive policies and practices" are defined in the legislation. This makes it difficult to determine what constitutes employment discrimination, and what constitutes effective redress for employment discrimination.
The second major problem with the present legislation is that it makes no reference to equal pay for work of equal value. Such groups as the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and the Canadian Labour Congress have urged that pay equity legislation be included in any employment equity plan. Judge Abella stated, "Equal pay is an integral element in the implementation of employment equity. It must be included in any undertaking by employers to make the practices in the workplace more equitable".

There has been for almost 10 years a federal law under which employers are required to pay the same salary to both men and women assuming similar functions.
However, redress of pay inequities depends essentially on complaints lodged by individual employees who feel discriminated against. But it is the employers who are responsible for eliminating pay disparities based on sex.
As for the Federal Government, it must introduce legislation positively requiring employers to implement a pay equity program. We know that if we rely on voluntary measures, women's salaries will be slow to improve.
Last summer the Canadian Human Rights Commission called upon the Government to introduce stronger pay equity legislation, specifically legislation which would require employers to work with employee representatives to implement pay equity measures.
We have seen the success of this collective approach to pay equity in Hamilton where an historic collective agreement was recently signed. The Canadian Union of Public Employees and the Hamilton School Board agreed to work together to develop a plan which would close the wage gap between female
cleaners and male caretakers within two years. Hopefully this agreement opened the door for other public service unions to bargain pay equity.
The role of bargaining and negotiation is neglected in the Government's employment equity legislation. While the employer is required to consult with the employee, there is no obligation to negotiate. I point out the large difference between consultation and negotiation. As the Hamilton example illustrates, unions have been at the forefront of the struggle for employment equity. The invaluable knowledge of the workplace that the union can provide must be recognized by requiring employers to negotiate with union representatives.
The present legislation is also flawed by its limited application to federal government contractors. It only applies to firms with 100 or more employees. It only applies if the contract exceeds $200,000, and it does not apply to construction. Firms seeking government contracts must only indicate their intention to implement the employment equity guidelines. They are not required to submit annual reports or workplace data. They are subject to random inspections to monitor compliance. No effective mechanism exists to enforce this legislation.
Finally, the legislation does not even apply to all federal departments. The Government claims that the departments not covered by the Act are already protected by adequate affirmative action plans. However, we know that these programs are totally management controlled. Many of them are not subject to bargaining under the Public Service Staff Relations Act. Most seek to promote some women to higher management positions, while they ignore the majority of women workers. Like the employment equity and equal pay legislation, they lack the force and commitment of law.
Judge Abella recommended that all federally regulated employers be included under the legislation, but the Government chose to ignore her recommendations. When we are talking about the convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women which the Minister tabled in the House, certainly Judge Abella's report was mentioned. However, what was not mentioned was the lack of legislation being introduced which was comprehensive enough to follow through on the recommendations.
Also I would like to look at some of the problems in employment equity, job training, and job re-entry. We know that the Canadian Jobs Strategy program specifically designed for women-they were the target group-required women to have spent at least three years out of the labour force to be eligible for training. This does not make any sense whatsoever. Many women who want to re-enter the labour force have spent much time in part-time, low-paying jobs. They had to do things to keep body and soul together and, therefore, they do not comply with the terms of reference for job re-entry.
We are also very concerned about the lack of language training for immigrant women. We know that a lawsuit has been launched respecting discrimination against immigrant
March 9, 1988

women who are not allowed to take language training. The Government has not seen fit to say that these women are eligible for language training even though they were certainly welcomed into the country. We look forward to them being a strong component of the country. We say, in terms of Canadian policies, that we want immigrant women to add to the fabric and rich culture of the country, yet we discriminate against them and do not allow them to have language training. The tensions and anxiety we put on these women are very difficult to document in that they are so vast. They need language skills and communications skills just to get their report cards from school, to talk to teachers, for home and school interviews, or to know what kinds of jobs are available to them in the workforce. It really is important, for them to become part of society, to be eligible for language training, but the Government has refused to incorporate that.
I would like to deal with single mothers who have looked at job re-entry. Very often these women find themselves in a situation where they have not been out of the workforce for three years. Often they are the sole bread-winners, whether they be separated, divorced, or widowed, yet they find themselves not eligible for job re-entry. I was dismayed when I heard at committee just this past week that it was thought that the eligibility recommendations should not be changed because it would cost too much. Well, it will cost much more if we relegate these women to a role of poverty and inability to participate in the labour force for many years. It is a very crucial matter as far as the whole program of Canadian Jobs Strategy is concerned.
The skills and shortage program of Canadian Jobs Strategy had a female participation rate of 8.5 per cent. It is a program with an abundance of non-traditional occupations for women. Clearly women continue to face substantial barriers in entering into non-traditional occupations, evidenced in regional employment and immigration managers being committed to the equity principle in differing degrees. Some of it is very discriminatory and very subjective depending upon region. Some areas of the country are encouraging women to enter non-traditional jobs and better paying occupations. However, there is need for an over-all national strategy to tackle the occupational segregation of women.
We also recognize that in some areas it is an attitudinal problem and that we must encourage women by telling them that there is a future for them and that they do not have to stay in low-paying jobs.
I should like to refer to some of the facts in the report of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. For example, in Newfoundland, four out of eleven re-entry programs teach office skills. In New Brunswick, all four re-entry projects teach home-making, clerical, and word processing skills. Six out of ten entry projects are for training to women in sales, food services and hospitality. 1 must say those are not non-traditional occupations. In Toronto, Ontario, 15 out of 16 re-entry projects were in sales, clerical occupations and health services. It is all very well to say that we are encouraging women to take
Supply
on non-traditional occupations but the reality is that it is not happening. In British Columbia and the Yukon 36 per cent of job development training provided to women was in the clerical, sales and service occupations. Nearly every one of the 20 re-entry projects was related to office skills and clerical occupations. Women are being ghettoized into job occupations that are low paying. They have little opportunity for advancement and they experience a very high rate of unemployment.
We have heard a lot from the Government about the kind of child care needed in the country. A task force was appointed but we did not need another task force. We knew that there were two million children in need of child care. The task force recommended the phasing in of a publicly funded universally accessible cost shared system between the federal and provincial Governments. We also know that that is not what the Government's progress report is to the United Nations. The Government said that it had appointed a task force, but the Government ignored the recommendations of the task force which makes a very different kind of report. Had the report been complete it would have shown the recommendations of the task force and what the possibilities for Canadian children of the future could have been. However, the national strategy on child care will not provide Canadian families with affordable, accessible quality child care.
We know that the child care strategy which the Conservative Government is talking about is a strategy that will allow for tax benefits to people who already have their children in child care. There are no national standards to ensure quality. Yet the task force cried out for the kind of national standards that would guarantee that people who are giving care to our children will be trained in what pre-school child development is all about.

The federal Government rejected the principle for national objectives determination in its child care plan. It is therefore quite possible day care services offered Canadian families will differ from one province to the next.

Fifty per cent of the strategy budget is allocated toward tax measures, such as the doubling of the child tax deduction which does not benefit any low-income families. Tax measures also do not result in an increase in day care spaces. There will remain important shortages in day care spaces. That surely is what the priority must be.
The Government intends to create 200,000 new day care spaces over seven years. This rate of increase is actually less than what we saw in 1974. The program limits the rate of increase of funds presently being put forward by the Government. It seems to me it is very clear that the Government is implementing the kind of legislation that will meet the needs of women of Canada. There has been absolutely no action on extended parental leave.

The New Democrats had hoped some measures would be initiated regarding long leaves of absence for parents who could then stay home with their young children. The Conservatives' strategy does not take that valid option into consideration for working parents.
Canadian families deserve a better national child care program. The New Democrats have asked that parents be offered real choices.
An equitable system must create a greater number of places for 1,800,000 children who need them. It will also have to try to help parents by allowing them to take long parental leaves of absence and by providing for more community resources.

If we really do believe that there will be equality for women in this country we have to recognize that there will be economic equality. There will never be economic equality if we do not provide adequate child care. To the present, at least in technology, women are the only ones who can produce children. If women can be competitive in the workforce outside the home it is imperative that they enter into the labour force without having concerns of what is happening to their children.
There are far too many latchkey children in the country today. There are far too many children who are being looked after in informal care. Some of it is very good but a lot of it is informal care and we do not really recognize the downfalls and the downsides until we see the results and we have had some tragedies already. We know the most crucial years are the first eight years of a child's life. We have known that for a long time. We are requiring child care workers to have two years post-secondary training, so surely we should not expect these people to work below the poverty line, but that is what is happening in Canada today.
If the Government is sincere about Canadian women having equal opportunity with men, the wage gap must be closed. We have to make sure that real opportunities and real choices for women are there in the labour force. We have to implement a child care program with national objectives and national quality in its delivery. If the Government were sincere, it would have implemented some of these things instead of shadow boxing with the legislation.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to clarify for the Hon. Member some things about the jobs strategy and employment equity that I think are important for the House to recognize.
In terms of employment equity, I think the Hon. Member does know that Rosie Abella, who prepared the very excellent employment equity report, was very pleased with the quick response of the Government to many of her recommendations. Our employment equity initiative continues to go into effect, I think, in a very positive way. In terms of trying to expand it or change it, let me say that mandatory annual reports are due in
June, 1988 and those reports will be available to the public. The failure to report can result in a $50,000 fine. I have been in business a long time, Mr. Speaker, and no company likes to pay that kind of a fine nor does a company like to be publicly embarrassed.
Under the federal contractors program, as of January 1, 1988, approximately 900 companies had signed certificates. By January 30, 44 companies had been reviewed and arrangements were in progress to review an additional 24 companies in accordance with on site compliance. This is very active. Companies that do not comply can be barred from future contracts. Bids from two companies which refused to comply have been rejected. We have been fortunate because we found in most cases that companies are prepared to comply when we put their feet to the fire. The program is working and it is a big incentive.
I want to talk briefly about the Canadian Jobs Strategy Program. Of the participants in job development, job entry, skill shortages, skill investment, training has been received in the following occupations: managerial, professional, semiprofessional, technical, supervisory and, for women, skill crafts trades and semi-skilled workers.
Women comprised 42.5 per cent of the Canadian Jobs Strategy participants last year and preliminary figures for this year indicate an increase to 44 per cent. Also, there has been $48.5 million in dependant care allowances directed to approximately 22,000 of these participants.
One very important point on the Canadian Jobs Strategy is its particular sensitivity to the needs of immigrant and native women because by transferring this severely employment disadvantaged option from job development to job entry it ensures easier access for native and immigrant women.
So that the Hon. Member is not expected just to take my word for this, I have a couple of letters from people who participated in the job entry program. One says:
In addition to just providing me with a formal education in a marketable skill the job re-entry program also made day care affordable, which in turn allowed me to attend daily classes. The job placement enabled me to put a recent previous employer on my resume. Without all three parts of this program I know that I would not be here, out in the work force, today.
Another woman writes:
-thanks again for giving me this wonderful opportunity to acquire this knowledge and self-confidence needed to get a job I really want and need. (1 was already offered an excellent position that I couldn't have dreamt about just a few months ago). I hope you will continue this program, so other women will get the same education I was privileged to get.
I want to leave the Hon. Member with these thoughts on the programs. She talked about the need to extend this program and about how many women are underemployed as well as unemployed. I certainly recognize that difficulty. We are, of course, trying to extend our resources as far as we can, given that our legacy from the previous Government is that 25 cents out of every tax dollar Canadians pay us goes to pay the
March 9, 1988

interest on the debt and is therefore not available for worthwhile programs such as these.

Mr. Speaker, it is all very well to say that reports will be filed this June, but the point I was trying to make was that though there is a punishment if reports are not filed, there is absolutely no punishment if the reports identify discrimination. There is nothing to remedy that. That is our major concern.
It is very good that some women have been able to take advantage of the Canadian Jobs Strategy, but the committee heard brief after brief from witness after witness indicating that women were mostly in job re-entry for the lower-paid jobs, the traditional jobs. As I said earlier, the Minister's own report of the advisory council indicates that 8.5 per cent of women were able to get non-traditional jobs. That is not adequate for equality for women in the economy.
It is important that we not use just one or two cases and say that these women have been successful. That is not what we are talking about. We are talking about the reality, about what the facts and figures show us, and the programs do need to be expanded. There is a limitation to the programs because women have to be out of the labour force for three years. Those are the kinds of things I would like the Minister to look at so that she may recommend to her colleague in Employment and Immigration that more women participate in the job reentry programs and that job skills be non-traditional skills so that women as well as men can get well paid jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to what my friend from Hamilton Mountain had to say. However, I do not want to let her speech go by without noting something from this side.
Not only did we hear brief after brief from women's group after women's group in city after city from one end of the country to the other when the Standing Committee of the Secretary of State was investigating funding for women's programs, but we produced a report entitled "Fairness in Funding". That report was unanimously adopted by members of all three Parties, including the Hon. Member's colleague from Vancouver East who made a very valuable contribution to that unanimous, all-Party report.
In essence, the report recognized all of the questions which were raised by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) in her remarks and also recommended that this Government, and I cannot think of any other Government before this one which has so urgently and responsibly addressed this matter, look at the bottom line as being equality of women in the workforce, in the market-place and in any way possible.
Our report contained a series of recommendations which would make it possible for women across Canada to address the very matters the Hon. Member has raised, matters I am sure the Hon. Member from the Liberal side will also raise. We wanted to make sure that women have access to the wide
Supply
range of programs that the Government is providing so that the bottom line will be equality for women in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly did appreciate the committee's unanimous report. We are looking for implementation of those recommendations as quickly as possible. Certainly some of the programs I addressed are the kind of programs that will put some substance into the report's recommendations.
Women across Canada have experienced the discrimination that has been dealt out over the years and are saying that they will not wait any longer, they need equity. I was addressing the programs that are in place now, programs which are not adequate to address the inequity that exists. Certainly, they are a first step but they are not enough.
We should not say that we have done enough and that women are now equal partners. It does not work if companies simply have to file reports. There must be some kind of implementation of the recommendations of reports like the one to which the Hon. Member referred. I believe the Hon. Member heard that as well while travelling with the committee.
Women do not want lip service any longer, they want action. They need money for programs and they need action. The work of the committee will certainly help, but we want the Government to implement stronger legislation.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House condemns the Government for its lack of progress in giving women a fair deal in the workplace and the labour market. We in the Liberal Party support the motion.
We support the motion because there is still too much systemic discrimination against women who try to enter certain trades and professions. We support the motion because there is still too great a gap between women's wages and men's wages, even when they are doing the same work or work of equal value. We support the motion because there are still too many barriers to women gaining access to training, especially training for non-traditional work. Finally, we support the motion because there are insufficient support programs for women who want to work or train. Here I have in mind in particular adequate day care programs, and my hon. colleague from Outremont will deal more fully with that subject when she speaks.
Yes, we should condemn the Government for this lack of progress. I will give details on each point I raised. The reason we have not had the progress we should have had is because the Government is basically a laissez-faire Government. It is basically a small "c" conservative Government that does not have the political will to do what it says is right.
Government members say the right things. They say that they are in favour of employment equity. They say that they are in favour of closing the wage gap. Then they introduce

Supply
half-measures to accomplish the goals they say they favour. They adopt measures which do not effectively accomplish the goals that they say are good goals. They talk a good game, but they do not follow it up with action.
A good example of this is the employment equity legislation which was passed in June of 1986, Bill C-62. That legislation does not provide for any sanctions whatsoever if the companies touched by the legislation do not advance employment equity or affirmative action for women. As my hon. colleague from Hamilton Mountain said, there are fines if the companies do not file reports indicating how many men, women and visible minorities are employed. However, if they do not progress along the road to employment equity, there are no sanctions. There are no fines.
Judge Rosalie Abella was appointed by the former Liberal Government in February of 1983 to study the whole problem of employment equity. She came to the conclusion that there was systemic discrimination against women and minorities in the workplace. She said there had to be enforceable legislation to correct that. The Government introduced a Bill but it did not provide what Judge Abella recommended, enforceable legislation with sanctions.
During the debate on that Bill, Bill C-62, we in the Liberal Party presented 36 amendments to make it stronger, provide enforceable mechanisms, and so on. Members on the government side voted down every amendment except for a few minor ones. As I said before, the Government talks a good game with respect to employment equity and the wage gap and all these other things, but it does not have the political will or political philosophy to do something effective about it.
Are these criticisms I am making just those of the opposition or just criticisms that we make in Parliament simply for the sake of criticizing? Let us look at the record to see who else makes these very same criticisms to show it is not just Liberal or NDP Members. Here we have a former Conservative Member of Parliament, then chairman of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, who said, as quoted in The Ottawa Citizen of June 26, 1987, that: "Human Rights Commission urges system of fines to enforce pay equity." It continues:
The Canadian Human Rights Act must be given teeth to force employers to pay women the same as men for work of equal value, Canada's chief Human Rights Commissioner says.
He went on to say:
It is time for a major shift in the way in which we pursue equal pay at the federal level.
That was not a Liberal or NDP Member, that was a former Conservative Member of Parliament who was then chairman of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. He saw that the legislation was not working. He pointed out that there are
300,000	women who work for federally-regulated employers and there was a 35 per cent wage gap relating to those women.
Then there is a 1986 report published by the Economic Council of Canada. It deals with women re-entering the labour force and training programs and was written by D. Boothby. What does it say? At page 42:
I conclude-that discrimination is a significant source of occupational differences between men and women.
He goes on to say:
While employment and immigration personnel do not select trainees for these programs, the use of federal funding makes it imperative to ensure that these programs are operated in a non-discriminatory manner.
He is talking about training programs and he said that was not being done at present. Again, those recommendations have not been acted upon. The Government did not act upon the recommendations of Judge Abella, Mr. Fairweather, or Mr. Boothby to strengthen the legislation.
In 1987, for the first time in 18 years, the wage gap between men and women widened. For 18 consecutive years the gap had been narrowing so that women's wages were getting closer to men's, but in 1986, under a Conservative Government, they widened for the first time. Thank goodness that last year they started to narrow again, but in 1986 the wage gap was $10,257. That is the largest gap in the history of Canada since statistics have been kept. Again, that is not Liberal or NDP Members speaking, that is StatsCan. If that rate of progress was to continue, it would take another 79 years for women's wages to equal men's wages for the same type of work. That indicates that a laissez-faire, small "c" conservative approach will not work. We need legislative action.
The Human Rights Commissioner called on the Government, as I said earlier, to introduce a federal law similar to the pay equity law introduced in Ontario. Eight months have gone by and nothing has been done. Here we have a situation where women have been put into traditional type jobs, are moving into service type jobs which are low-paying, non-union, often at minimum wage, and without pension, health or other benefits. Many of them are single working mothers taking care of children all by themselves.
As a result of this growing wage gap, we are seeing a growing poverty rate under this Conservative Government. I have not a Liberal or NDP report, but a report put out by the National Council on Welfare in November, 1987. It pointed out that over one million children in Canada live in poverty. It referred to StatsCan figures which show that in 1986 there were 1,016,000 children under 16, more than one out of six, who were members of families whose incomes were below the poverty line. It points out that while that proportion, 17.6 per cent, is down from the peak of 20.8 per cent in 1984 during the recession, it is still higher than the rate in 1981, before the recession, of 16.5 per cent. Under the Conservative Government we have a rate of families living under the poverty line greater than prior to the recession in 1982.
The figures also point out that the average income for a family with a single parent taking care of the children was $17,353, compared to $44,919 for two-parent families. That is quite a gap. Between 1971 and 1981 single-parent families headed by women increased by almost 60 per cent. The number of those families now amounts to approximately 600,000.
March 9, 1988

It is not just these figures that point out this very sad state of affairs. 1 refer to an article in the Montreal Gazette dated October 17, 1987, following a study on poverty done by an investigative reporter in the year. It was found that there were more soup kitchens in Montreal than there were during the depression of the 1930s. We have several in my own constituency and it is a very sad state of affairs. A large number of those people are women who have been abandoned or divorced, single mothers taking care of families with no other resources except welfare, which is not sufficient, and they have to use soup kitchens.
1 have further evidence that these programs which the Government is very proud of are not working. I have a report by la Federation des femmes du Quebec which says the economic future of women in Quebec and the rest of Canada appears more cloudy than rosy. They point out that women are being relegated more than in the past to job ghettos. Nothing is being done to take them out of those ghettos and the programs of the Government are not working.
There are several studies on this subject which back up the contention that progress is not being made in employment equity despite the boasts and bragging of the Government. On that point, in statements which Ministers of the Government make in the House in answer to our questions and in debates such as the one which is taking place today, they keep glossing over the problem and presenting the picture in a very rosy way. One would think that they would finally realize that that is not being bought by the Canadian people, that it is not credible.
These reports tell why it is not credible. For the last two years the Government has been down in the polls. It has been down to 23 per cent, up to 27 per cent and 30 per cent, and back down to 27 per cent. One would think they would realize that people are not believing them.
I am sure that the Minister will get up and say what a rosy place Canada is because the Conservatives are doing so many wonderful things. She compares what is happening in 1988 to figures from the depths of the recession of 1982 and 1983 to show what great progress she has made. However, she does not compare the figures of 1988 with either 1980 or 1981 or the period which I pointed out the other day, 1970 to 1975.
If she wants to compare the Conservative record with the Liberal record let her do it over a period of years. She will find that the rate of unemployment under Liberal Governments from 1965 to 1980 was 5.6 per cent. In 1981, the year before the recession, the rate of unemployment was 7.5 per cent. The rate has now been reduced to 8.1 per cent, four years after the recession, and they think they have done a wonderful job.
Everyone knows that during the recession of 1982-83 there were high rates of unemployment in the United States, Britain,
Supply
Belgium, Holland and all over the world. The Minister should know that we are living in an interdependent world economically. The great crash of last October did not take place only in New York City. The crash of stock markets took place in Toronto, London, Tokyo, and around the world.
One could go on for a long while criticizing the programs of the Government. With regard to the Canadian Jobs Strategy, we on the Standing Committee of Labour, Employment and Immigration have been doing a study of that program for the last two or three months and are going to issue a report very soon in which we will show the inadequacy of the program.
The Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) who just spoke pointed out some of the inadequacies including the program's inflexibility and its targeting on groups such as women's groups. It is just not working the way it should. One of the harshest reports which the Auditor General ever made was his report last October with regard to the Canadian Jobs Strategy. It is not doing the things that it should do and it should be changed. I think the committee will make a unanimous report which will point to those failings in the program and call on the Government to change it.
If the Government is serious about employment equity, let us see something which will strengthen the legislation which we now have. Let us see the Government bring forward amendments and act on the recommendations which Mr. Fairweather made last summer as Chairman of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. Let the Government amend the employment equity Bill to provide enforcement mechanisms and wider coverage than it presently has, such as Judge Abella recommended. The Government did not do what Judge Abella recommended. She recommended that there be enforceable employment equity legislation rather than the wishy-washy type of legislation which we have. Let the Government put something into the legislation which will mandate a program of equal pay for work of equal value.
If the Government did those things it might see its credibility improve and it might see its fortunes go up in the polls. That may be bad for us in the Opposition but it would be good for the Canadian people because they would realize that when the Government says something it means it and it does it. However, up until now the Government has said one thing and has come forward with half measures, wishy-washy measures which are not accomplishing what it says it wants to accomplish.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am a little disappointed that the Hon. Member suggests that every time we stand up over here we suggest that things are really rosy. I do not think we have ever suggested that. We have suggested that we are trying to ensure that things continue to get better for women. That is an entirely different kind of debate.

March 9, 1988
Supply
One of the reasons that we have worked so hard to ensure that things get better for women is because things have not been good for women in Canada, certainly throughout my lifetime and certainly throughout the tenure of the previous Government. You can pick any year you like. You can talk about the prosperity between 1965 and 1970. I was in the workforce at that time and I do not recall that it was a singularly wonderful time to be a woman working in Canada with regard to discrimination, employment equity, and wage gap. I do not recall the then Government, which is now the Opposition, saying one single word to help me as a working woman in Canada.
I am a little bit bemused because members of the Government are trying to ensure that women are prepared with flexible career opportunities and child care. Child care was first declared an urgent matter in 1970 by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. I do not recall a whole lot being done between 1970 and 1984. When we came into power we appointed a parliamentary committee to travel across Canada to talk to women and other people who were interested in child care. Out of that came a strategy which will meet the needs of Canadians. We did that within three years. It did not take us 17 years. Whereas I am quite prepared to accept that things are not all rosy across Canada for women, I know that the Government has increased the momentum for women quite considerably.
As well, in terms of women being poor, the Hon. Member quoted some poverty statistics from Montreal. We are very aware of this and that is one of the reasons that we have tried to enhance training and apprenticeship programs with the provinces. The number of adult women living below the poverty line increased by 227,000 between 1981 and 1984 during the Liberal-induced recession.
Our economy during that recession was considerably worse than that of other countries. We suffered much more severely as a result of that recession, in part because of Liberal Government policies, because the deficit had run away with us long before the recession ever began, because of the National Energy Program, and because of other things done by that Government. That was harder on women, as things always are, than it was on other Canadians.
The number of adult women living below the poverty line in the last three and a half years has fallen by 178,000. I would hope that the Hon. Member would be happy to celebrate that.
I am delighted to hear it.
The wage gap has taken a little downturn and I remain concerned about that 34-cent gap; we must continue to work toward an improvement of that. That means, of course, moving women into non-traditional jobs as well as employment equity and so on.

Mr. Speaker, I did not realize that the previous Liberal Government had so much power, that we were able to induce a recession not only in Canada but in
Britain where the rate of unemployment went to over 13 per cent and in Belgium where it went to over 14 per cent. The entire western world had extremely high rates of unemployment at that time. Anyone who looks at the statistics will see that they jumped significantly in all those countries from 1981 to 1982 and started coming down in 1983-84.
When the Hon. Member says she cannot recall anything being done in 17 years, I do not know where she was. It seems to me that a very significant measure was passed in 1982. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights was passed by this Parliament, by a Liberal Government, which has led to some landmark decisions with respect to women. I could point to the establishment of the Canadian Human Rights Act in 1978, the Affirmative Action Program in the Public Service in 1983, the ratification of the Convention of the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women in December 1981.
I would refer the Minister to a short booklet put out by the Library of Parliament. It is entitled Unemployment in Canada-Its Differential Impact by Age and Sex. It lists a long number of things, going back to the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in 1967, all of which were accomplished by Liberal Governments.
I admit that the Minister and perhaps some of the people in the Government do not say that things are rosy all the time. However, if one listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and some others, one would think this country is nirvana under the Conservatives.
1 would agree with the Minister that she is trying to improve things, but the difference between her Conservative Party and our Party is that we, in trying to improve things, are willing to legislate enforceable laws to do so. The Party opposite is not willing to do that. It says it wants to get rid of discrimination in employment for women but it introduces a law with no enforceable mechanism.
Yes, the Conservatives are advancing slowly, bit by bit, but if they did what Judge Abella recommended, it would advance much faster. That is exactly what the motion before the House says. It criticizes the Government for its failure to make significant progress. If the Government did what Judge Abella and Gordon Fairweather, the former chairman of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, recommended and legislate enforceable mechanisms to get rid of discrimination against women, things would move faster. Things are moving too slow under this Government.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly found the Hon. Member's comments very instructive and agreed with many of them. I would like to remind the Hon. Member, however, that it was not just one Party that was dedicated to ensuring that women would be recognized in the Charter. I do believe it was the women of all Parties who fought very hard to ensure that the equality of women was included in the Charter.
March 9, 1988

I would like to ask a question with respect to affirmative action about which the Hon. Member commented. As I recall, in 1984, the Leader of the Liberal Party at a meeting of Liberal women said that he did not support affirmative action for women in the private sector. "Instead", he said, "I prefer to negotiate such goals on the basis of goodwill". In the past, goodwill has not really done much for the women of Canada. The Charter debate, to which 1 referred earlier, I think is a very good example of that. Does the Hon. Member's Party still consider that voluntary programs are an appropriate response to the systemic discrimination that women face in employment?

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure, but I think we were debating the employment equity Bill before the Hon. Member came to this House. As I mentioned in my remarks, our Party moved 36 amendments, one of which was to make employment equity and affirmative action enforceable for all those industries under federal jurisdiction.
It may be that in the election campaign of 1984 our Leader took that position, but we had discussed this at great length in our caucus over the two years prior to that legislation coming in. We looked at the Abella report and became convinced that the only way to solve the problem was by enforceable legislation. We took that position and moved those amendments.
On the Hon. Member's other point, I would agree there was among women in Canada, and among minorities in general, great support for an entrenched Charter of Rights. However, I was simply responding to the Minister when she said she could not recall anything being done in 17 years. If I had the time I could have put on the record a large number of things.
The problem, of course, is that we all know, for example, that in 1950 only 23.2 per cent of women were in the workforce. It was as we moved into the 1960s that women decided they wanted to work and then ran up against problems of discrimination, lack of day care, and so on. Then Governments had to start dealing with these problems.
As time went on it became necessary for parliaments and governments to deal with these issues. That is why in 1967, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, who was Prime Minister at the time, set up the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. From that time on this Party has introduced some of the recommendations. We have been moving ahead. However, I think there is a big difference between the Minister's Party and our Party in that she takes a more laissez-faire attitude. She is also the Minister of Privatization-let the private sector do it. We do not believe that. We believe we need legislation in certain cases. That marks the difference between the Liberal and Conservative Parties.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to speak today against this motion as presented by the Hon.
Supply
Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar). As a member of this Government, and as a woman, I am somewhat bemused that the Hon. Member would condemn our Government for its efforts to eliminate discrimination against women in Canada. This Government has made more progress in enhancing women's equality in Canada than any Government, in fact, more than all previous Governments combined.

Our Goverment and our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) certainly did not opt for the path of least resistance, as the Hon. Member implied in her attack on the Government. The Prime Minister was very demanding in the objectives he set for this Government. He promised we would double the percentage of women appointed, from 15 per cent to 30 per cent, and we have reached that objective. In Cabinet alone, there are five women, and there are now more women judges, ambassadors and deputy ministers, as well as senior officials responsible for policy development and decision-making.

Today I can reinforce what my colleague, the Hon. President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), said today, that the federal Government has reached its first major hiring target for women in the management category of the Public Service. The Government has been striving to more than double the number of women in the management category from 217 in 1983 to 475 by March 31, 1988. As of yesterday, we are beyond 475. There are now 509 women in the management category. I think the Government is to be congratulated.
We are now about to set new targets for the next three years. We will see, I think, a more positive momentum forward. Special training in employment programs within the Government is being provided, with 250 person-years and $8.8 million over five years to assist women in pursuing nontraditional occupations. Together with 13 Public Service unions, the Government has launched one of the largest equal pay studies ever, involving more than 4,400 employees. The results will be available in late 1989.
If all of this had been in place when we came to office, we could be moving forward a little more rapidly. But we are doing, I think, extraordinarily well because our Government does not talk about equality, we do something about it. Unlike the Hon. Member whose motion this is, we do not believe that women must continue to be presented only as victims. We are determined to create a social and economic environment in which women can be full participants, as they deserve to be, and in which women can contribute to the full extent of their skills and their talents.
We do not believe that the state or the Government can manage every aspect of a woman's life better than the woman herself. The NDP would like to help women. They would like to give women everything except opportunity and the choice for women to be themselves.

March 9, 1988
Supply
[ Translation]
We do not believe women are all alike, and we praise their differences. There are women who choose to work in the home and women who want to work outside the home. There are women who earn their living in traditional occupations, and there are women who have been pioneers in forestry, engineering, architecture and even in space.

We are no longer living in the early 1900s when women did not have the vote. They had to fight and fight to get it. Nor is it 1929 when women had to fight and fight to be declared persons. This is not the 1950s when women who served overseas or who worked in factories during the war returned home and stayed home. It is not even the 1960s when women organized themselves into what we now call the contemporary women's movement.
This is the 1980s. Women do not and will not take a back seat to anyone. Issues that once were never discussed in public, issues such as family violence, sexual harassment, defaulting spouses and unequal pay are now front and centre, not only because women have put them there, which they have, but also because women have developed allies, women and men who will do something about these issues.
The Hon. Member who presents the motion condemns our Government in the area of child care. Let me correct just one point in this area. When I said nothing had been done I referred to the Royal Commission on the Status of Women which declared child care an urgent matter in 1970. What was done about child care? That was the point that I made earlier, and I will repeat it now. Nothing-nothing was done about child care, except there was a great deal of talk, promise and more spending on other items by the former Government so that it became less and less affordable; and another whole generation grew up.
Our Government has acted. We have a national child care strategy that will create over 200,000 new subsidized child care spaces. We will provide support to families, whatever their preferred choice for providing care to their children. Choice is the key word.
This is a telling difference between our Government and the Parties opposite. We believe that Canadians everywhere know best how child care should be provided. That is why we have a special child care initiatives fund that will provide $100 million worth of assistance to Canadians to meet the child care needs of special situations such as children who are ill, children who are disabled, as well as the needs of rural women, seasonal workers and those in other situations which we expect will be brought forward. I refer to items such as culturally-centred child care.

As a Government, we want to act as partners with the parents, day care experts, teachers and provincial and municipal governments-with all parties that have an important role
to play in this sector. We do not intend to lay down a single set of rules for what is good for every child in Canada.

If giving women in families a choice in child care is discrimination then, yes, we are guilty. If putting billions of dollars where others put volumes of rhetoric and promises is discrimination then, yes, we are guilty. If trusting in the good sense of Canadians to know what is best for their children is discrimination then, yes, we are guilty. If the definition of discrimination by Members opposite is choice, concerted action and faith in individual Canadians and their families then, alas, yes, we have failed. But I believe that the hundreds of thousands of Canadian women, men and children who will benefit from our child care initiative will tell the Hon. Member and her Party that they are tired of outdated definitions, false accusations and hollow condemnations.
Our Party has shown common sense and the practical management experience to shake the Canadian economy out of the doldrums that threatened to mortgage the lives of our children and our grandchildren and make child care not affordable.

The NDP would keep women in traditional jobs. Under the NDP, women would have to pay their union dues but their advancement to executive positions would be blocked.

While we are talking about unions, let me just point out that women comprise 36.2 per cent of union membership and only 19.3 per cent of union executive boards. That figure is up by only 1 per cent since 1978. So where is the union leadership and the leadership of the NDP?
By working with the private sector we are able to make a great many changes. The federal Government has set up a joint program with the Canadian Construction Association- and someone mentioned construction earlier-to look at the barriers to women entering that field. This is the first time ever that the Government and the private sector have taken a sectoral approach to this problem. This is a project worth $345,000, much of which is being paid by the federal Government in order to ensure that in that non-traditional sector there will be more momentum. This is the best way we can get at the wage gap.
No, the Hon. Member opposite and her Party are not the great protectors of women, any more than those Members of the last Government that mumbled on and on for all those years are the great protectors of women. Let me say that the Hon. Member who has presented this motion has worked for women and for women's issues long and hard throughout her career. I have a great deal of respect for her and her point of view.
However, in terms of our Party, we realize that there can be no social progress unless we have the economic framework that can support the development and the expansion that is
March 9, 1988

necessary for women who comprise 52 per cent of our population to be contributors, as they want to be. That is why we have worked hard on a program of economic renewal. It is why we made our first objective jobs, a tangible, measurable indicator of performance.
Have we performed? Some 1,156,0000 jobs have been created since 1984. Of those jobs 611,000 went to women, 85 per cent of them full time. Compare that to the fact that under the previous Government-and pick your time, Mr. Speaker- only 20 per cent of new jobs created were full time. We have broadened the opportunities for women by expanding, training and skills development through the Canadian Jobs Strategy. We have made special provision for the needs of immigrant women and visible minority women.
[ Translation]
We have also used our influence as an employer to accelerate women's equality on the labour market. We passed the Employment Equity Act, obliging Crown corporations and federally regulated businesses to implement employment equity programs under which women and visible minorities are offered better employment opportunities. Corporations and businesses which have one hundred or more employees must set objectives, establish action plans and time frames, and submit annual reports. The legislation affects about 1,000 businesses with over 950,000 employees. This is a major step towards employment equity.
The federal contractors program requires companies with 100 or more employees that bid on federal contracts worth $200,000 or more to introduce employment equity. We mean business. They are subject to on site compliance. We have already invoked this clause a number of times for multimillion dollar contracts where bidders were not compliant.
I believe that it is more than evident that on the matter of our Government's record on employment equity, the Member's motion flies in the face of reality. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, in response to the previous Member of the Official Opposition who spoke, that the number of low income women in Canada has declined by 5.7 per cent. By pushing away on all those factors we are making it better for women.
The Member raises the question of programs for native women. That is something that I personally regard as very important, as does our Government. With the passage of Bill C-31 discrimination on the basis of sex has been eliminated from the Indian Act. There are more than 45,000 native women who are taking advantage of this. That was something that native women had requested many years ago. We went even further last year for the first time by making the aboriginal women's program a permanent program. That signals our long-term commitment to supporting the full social, cultural, and political participation of aboriginal women in Canadian society. In 1986-87 alone, 69 groups, 87 projects, received
Supply
support under this program on a wide range of issues of particular interest to native women.
As a Government we are committed to the native peoples of Canada, women and men, and we will continue to work towards a better future for our native peoples, protecting the cultural heritage of their own traditions and respecting women within that native community.
I could go on and deal with other areas that have eliminated long-standing forms of discrimination against women, such as family order enforcement, pension reform, and new roles for women in the military.
I would like to conclude with a statement of our Party's over-all philosophy in the matter of discrimination against women. It is our view that women represent not only 52 per cent of the population in Canada, but 52 per cent of the total capabilities of this country, the talents and skills that we have. Any law, policy, or measure that restricts women's full equality lessens our effectiveness as a nation. Our Party will continue to work for the full legal, social, economic, and political equality of women. We will not rest until that equality has been achieved.
Hear, hear!

I wish to comment a little and ask a question of the Minister. The Conservative Government has done a lot of talking, and perhaps a certain amount of putting in place of reports, but there has been very little action or leadership as far as a number of areas are concerned. I particularly want to talk about the area of child care. There is still a major shortage of child care spaces. The Government's policy, of which it speaks a lot but on which it has not taken much action, will not increase the number of child care spaces any faster than they were being increased before.
Low income people who need the child care do not get any tax breaks. In many cases, they are unable to make use of the breaks that are available to them. There is no parental leave established in the sense that it be made available for those people who need it the most. There are no increased resources to the community which would support parents in the home. The $200 tax break is quite inadequate for anyone who needs to make use of it. There has been a lot of talk about what the Government intends to do, or what it will do sometime in the future, but very little action or real movement toward making child care available to the people who really need it.
That is the type of smoke and mirrors which this Government seems to think is good enough to treat the really major problems of women who want to be in the workforce.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext: In terms of action, it is very important to know what the Government has done on child care. We have a national child care strategy, something that we have never had in this country before.

No action.

March 9, 1988

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
The Hon. Member knows that this has to be negotiated with the provinces. It is under provincial jurisdiction. The Hon. Member also knows that funding will be available as of the next fiscal year starting April 1. The funding is there and it is in place, as soon as the details can be worked out with the provinces. This is an enormous step forward.
The Hon. Member made reference to the myth of the NDP that spaces would have increased faster under the old system. There were several things wrong with the old system. First, the shared cost program with the provinces meant that hardly any of the provinces could afford to increase child care any faster. Second, it was under the Canada Assistance Plan. That provided some relief, but it was essentially a welfare-based program. This is not a welfare issue. This is a national issue of some significance. By taking all of that and moving it into a new child care strategy, we have given child care a life of its own on a national scale. This is a seven-year program, but at the end of that seven years it will continue. There will be more to be done.
I know that the Hon. Member comes from an agricultural area. In developing this strategy we were very sensitive to the particular needs of farm women, who need child care perhaps 24 hours a day during the planting and harvesting seasons and perhaps not much in between, but their pattern is very different from those of women. With the special initiatives fund they have been given an opportunity to develop the types of solutions that they need when the nearest town may be 40 miles away, or when they are helping their husbands in the field.
Our national child care strategy is an attempt to be sensitive to different needs across Canada in little communities, in big communities, in isolated regions, for farm women, shift workers, and so on. It is a very exciting step forward on behalf of the women of Canada and, more particularly of course, for the children of Canada.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for the status of women mentioned that a seven year program would be targeted at specific projects and would be made available to people as of April 1.
However, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) tolds us, when the Government tabled its answer in the House that these funds were definitely earmarked for special programs over a seven year period, but should they all be used up after two years, the programs would have to be terminated.
Therefore, I would like the Minister to tell us whether it would not have been better to put a little more money in the programs, in child care spaces rather than allocating funds to programs where in a matter of perhaps two years, there would not be any money left.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
In our program we have come up with a balanced approach. Women who stay at home and work in the home and care for their children also deserve some consideration. We found when we discussed this with the women across Canada that they expressed some frustration around a space being the only answer. Not everyone wants to put their child into a child care space. We recognize the need for spaces, and we want them to grow as fast as we can develop a program for better spaces and more spaces. We know that the provinces' ability to fund these spaces varies from one province to another. It is up to us to try to help them meet their objectives as well as our national objective.
Women at home, women who want time to be with their children, deserve some recognition as well. That is one part of the tax side. Of course the other is a tax with receipted expenses to allow people to take advantage of it and to recognize better than before the legitimate costs. It used to be that the maximum one could claim against tax was $2,000. We have doubled that amount for pre-school children to $4,000. It is another area which should have been changed a long time ago to reflect the reality of the workplace.
With the combination of our tax provisions, our special initiatives fund, which is sensitive to needs across Canada, and the new spaces which will be developed, we are seeing a momentum in this area that we have never before seen in Canada. It will carry us further over the next seven years and will recognize that child care is an issue for all Canadians- women working outside the home, women working in the home, and fathers. We want to work with all of them because, of course, it is on behalf of our children.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to follow up on child care spaces. A $200 tax credit is certainly not adequate to encourage a mother to stay at home. For either a mother or father to stay at home for a $200 tax credit per annum is an insult to the value of the work he or she does. Tax breaks do not come to low-income families.
When we are stressing the need for more spaces, we are talking about a variety of ways; they can be flexible. However, for goodness' sake, let us look at reality and recognize the fact that children need an identifiable unit of care. This is what we are really talking about. I do not think that a tax break actually provides that. It is really important to clarify it, because low-income families will not benefit from it.
Does the Minister have a commitment to ensuring that the federal Government will respond to the Canadian Human Rights Commission by bringing forth the effective and mandatory pay equity legislation for which it asked?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the child care issue, the credit will be $700, not $200. This was an augmentation, and we recognize that it is not an income replacement program.
March 9, 1988

As far as spaces for women who are poor are concerned, there are a number of ways in which they are helped. One is that they qualify for subsidized space. Second, if they are taking a training program, they frequently get a child care allowance. There are many ways to help them.
Let me say, in terms of the pay equity provisions of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, that we will be watching how it works over the next while. We are pleased that the Canadian Human Rights Commission is monitoring the situation. In fact, I met with the Human Rights Commissioner just today, and we discussed a number of issues affecting the status of women in Canada. We recognize very much their role, but I think it is premature to move into some new aspect when things are clearly getting considerably better. We do not want to come down with a great anvil on a situation that we think will be considerably better over the next few years.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on the motion of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar). As one who has also been involved, as have many Hon. Members in the House, in the women's movement for a number of years, it seems that each year we keep discovering women again and discovering new aspects of women. We have shown some progress over the years. Women are represented in the labour force in greater numbers. There has been legislation to reflect that, and there have been programs to reflect that. As I said, I am pleased to speak today on the motion because there is still lots to do. I do not suspect that the Minister or anyone else would disagree with that.
I should like to address two specific areas which I think illustrate perhaps different reasons for putting forth the motion today. The first one deals with Bill C-31 and Section 12(1 )(b) of the Indian Act, to which I believe the Minister referred. For those who are not familiar with it, it is an example of legislation brought in to redress discrimination. I think it was a very positive measure. The purpose was to allow women who lost their Indian status through marriage to regain that status and membership in bands upon application, as well as their dependent children and first generation children. It was a positive aspect to address discrimination, and I will expand on some of the problems that I see in that regard.
The second issue about which I would like to talk is the trade policy of the Government that is directed generally to the economy and how it impacts negatively on certain sectors of the women's community perhaps more severely than on others. It addresses this motion not because it has an aspect of discrimination per se, but certainly the fall-out from such a policy will, in my view, have a discriminatory effect on women in certain segments.
The struggle for equality for women is not over. It is ever continuing. As I mentioned, the two issues about which I will speak highlight that.

Turning to Bill C-31 and Section 12(1 )(b) affecting aboriginal women, it is an example of a piece of legislation brought in to redress discrimination, to correct some of the discriminatory actions of past legislation. When the Indian Act first came in, women were seen as chattels of their spouses and, therefore, their rights were not considered. If they married a non-aboriginal person they lost their status. We now recognize that that was certainly an historical mistake in attempting to redress it.
The problem is not that the intent is not good. The problem is that we must have adequate resources committed to implementing the intent of such legislation. We are sadly lacking in this area. There has been a problem right from the start of the two years that Bill C-31 has been in effect in ensuring that the legislation can be implemented in a fair and just way. I should mention, first of all, the fact that there were not adequate resources. We see this now in the areas of housing, post-secondary education, and in the simple processing of applications.
I would mention, for example, that in February of this year a constituent of mine, Jean Gleason, who also happens to be on the executive of the Native Women's Association of Canada, representing 95,987 native Canadians, came to Ottawa to speak to the committee on Bill C-31. In a February 23, 1988 article in The Toronto Star, she is quoted as identifying a number of the problems that she sees with the implementation of the legislation. What she mentions, for example, is that native Canadians are being required to do great amounts of research to prove their status. She says that someone had to find birth certificates of relations. Others have had to retain lawyers to help them wade through the paperwork required. This, as we see, does not enable women to take advantage of these attempts to redress discrimination. Miss Gleason and the Native Women's Association of Canada at that time were urging the Government to hire more staff to work through the great backlog of applications. They were hoping that the Government would look at such things as more toll-free telephone lines and would hire native Canadians to work in this field helping people find appropriate documentation for their status applications.
It is clear, and the Government has said on several occasions, that the number of people re-applying for Indian status was greatly underestimated. Now is the time to put in adequate resources so people who are re-applying can take advantage.
I would like to go on a little bit about the problems when adequate resources are not committed to legislation. As we all know, Sandra Lovelace a number of years ago went to the United Nations and began this fight for the rights of Indian women. Mary Two-Axe Early was also involved and was a great leader. At great personal expense they have carried on and paved the way for the bringing in of such legislation.

March 9, 1988
