As Miss Gleason pointed out in her presentation at the committee, there is great concern within the Department of Indian Affairs among its employees about the inability to process applications, thus creating a huge backlog, with the result that many people are not receiving the benefits to which they are entitled. Nowhere does this inadequacy of funding become more apparent than in the area of housing. It is a well-known fact in this country that housing on Indian reserves and the money available for housing has been woefully inadequate. We have some of the most shocking housing situations on reserves, and the resources have not been committed to addressing that. Housing is a right under the Indian Act. The Government does have an obligation to provide housing for aboriginal people. Under Bill C-31, with the reinstatement of a number of new additions to the band list, the need for housing has simply increased exponentially.
So we have a situation which is very, very serious and is creating another kind of social situation. What about new people who are being added to a community who, in a sense, achieve some special status, in this case under Bill C-31, and who may receive funding for housing while others who have been waiting do not? This is a very serious problem in some communities but not in all. Again, we come back to the issue of not putting in adequate resources to implement nondiscriminatory legislation.
In a second area there are such issues as post-secondary education. Many aboriginal people and groups themselves have talked about the necessity to increase educational and training resources for their people so they can become self-sufficient. But there are inadequate funds in the Budget for postsecondary education. We see many people who may take advantage of this benefit and who have the right to take advantage of this benefit under the legislation but who are unable to do so because the Government says, "Sorry, we have run out of money". This is just not good enough. It is not good enough to have the words and not the resources.
A number of groups have commented on this. For example, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women in March this year in presenting its brief to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, mentioned the need for housing resources and post-secondary resources. There were a number of recommendations that would, I think, ease the situation if the resources were committed. Another issue in the brief is that the funds of the Department of Indian affairs are not available for many applicants who wish or need to take their cases to court if they feel there are violations to the law. Funds should be available so women who have rights given to them by law can take advantage of them.
In The Toronto Star for October 29, 1987, Ontario leaders were charging that again Parliament and the Government had not lived up to its promise, that it had not put in the resources, that the resources of Indian bands and reserves were being strained and this was creating both dissension within the community as well as unfairness to women.
There are many ways to look at the question of discrimination. We applaud such things as Section 12(l)(b) of the Indian Act and Bill C-31, but things are only as good as the funds the Government is willing to commit to implement legislation.
Second, I want to say a few words about the potential effects of the trade deal on certain women in the workforce. Poverty, as we know, has largely been shown to be a female phenomenon-I think the Minister referred to that this afternoon- whether it is single mothers, working mothers or working mothers who are having trouble getting child care. I believe that about 66 per cent of those who live under the poverty line are women. It is my contention that the trade deal will seriously impact on many of them. I want to mention certain sectors. First, the manufacturing sector. In a recent release from the Canadian Labour Congress, it was shown that women comprised 51 per cent of the workforce in poultry products, 62 per cent in leather products, and 79 per cent in the clothing industry. We know from the Government's own studies that these sectors will be most severely impacted by the trade deal. We have large numbers of women working in those sectors.
About 83 per cent of women who are employed work in the service sector, including education and health, social services, transportation, advertising, banking and so on. Here is another sector which will be severely impacted. In an Ontario study it was estimated that 44 per cent of the women in the manufacturing sector were at risk, while 27.6 per cent of men in that same sector were at risk.
I would like to address some areas that we see are in jeopardy under this trade deal and which will lead to further discrimination against women. For many years, Parties have worked for legislation, such as maternity benefits, minimum wage, health and safety regulations and employment standards. Many of the women in the manufacturing and service sectors are not unionized. Those women are relying on government legislation to protect their right to ward off deterioration in health and safety in the workplace. Under the trade deal these things could be in jeopardy if our trading partners were to say they are unfair subsidies. We want a level playing field. Women have never had a level playing field. This trade deal will not make a level playing field for women. It will simply increase the already existing imbalance.
I believe the Minister mentioned this afternoon that about 32 per cent of unionized workers are women. I am sure that this is quite true. When people have job dislocation-and the Government's own studies have indicated dislocation in this sector-women have not fared nearly as well as men in reemployment. For example, one Ontario study indicated that after job dislocation in a number of sectors, 72 per cent of men were re-employed but only 62 per cent of women.
In many sectors, we often see immigrant women, women whose first language may not be French or English. We see
March 9, 1988

women who have less transferable skills. There are no unskilled women, only those with perhaps less transferable skills. These are the women who will have difficulty finding reemployment.
I mentioned earlier that it is legislation that has protected many women in the workplace. Unions have also fought for many of these benefits. We have seen through further studies on dislocation that unionization is often reduced by about 30 per cent as there is a greater pressure to decrease wages and be more competitive.
These are important impacts on women in the workplace. For example, today we had a fair degree of discussion about the GATT ruling on the West Coast fisheries. This is a situation that exemplifies what I am talking about, namely, sectoral impacts on women. About 70 per cent of those working in fish-processing plants are women. Many of them represent that group I just mentioned, immigrant women, women who will require considerable retraining to take a place in the job market.
That brings me to another factor of history from which we can learn in the issue of impacts on women leading to more discriminatory measures. The Canadian Jobs Strategy program has been referred to in the debate this afternoon. It has not been a great success for women. The Canadian Jobs Strategy has not attacked the needs for upgrading and for literacy skills or many of the other specific training needs. In the attempt to privatize the training sector by moving funds over to private industry, we are shortchanging these people, many of whom are women.
We see here some very serious potential difficulties. I received a letter from one of my constituents, Joyce Hayden, who expressed her concern about the impact of this trade deal on older women. Again, older women tend to be the last hired and the first fired. We have also seen that adjustment programs for older workers promised by the Government have not come into effect. Again, this group of women will be very negatively affected.
In supporting this motion, we have to be very aware of two things. First, we must put the resources behind the rhetoric. As well, and the Minister said this this afternoon, when there is dislocation, women are often impacted very severely.
I would like to end on a more hopeful note by quoting some statistics. As usual, the Government of the Yukon is leading the way, being a New Democratic Government. The report of the Secretary of State on the elimination of forms of discrimination against women contains some very interesting statistics. The number of women represented in legislatures across Canada range from about 2 per cent in Newfoundland to 7 per cent in Ontario and 10 per cent in British Columbia, but in the Yukon, it is 18.7 per cent, topping the list. The representation of women on municipal councils, in the positions of mayors and councillors, ranges from about 8.5 per cent in Manitoba, 6.4 per cent in Ontario, 13 per cent in Prince Edward Island, and 33.3 per cent in the Yukon. The representation of women
Supply
on school boards is 35 per cent in Quebec but it is 56.2 per cent in the Yukon. Finally, federal appointments to provincial, territorial and lower courts range from 6.1 per cent in British Columbia to 6.3 per cent in Alberta, zero per cent in the Northwest Territories, I am sad to say, 4 per cent in Saskatchewan and 33.3 per cent in the Yukon.
Where there is a will there is a way. We need to put some teeth into anti-discriminatory legislation and we need to look forward to more programs which will effectively eliminate all forms of discrimination against all women in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague from the Yukon for her very clear positions on how women are suffering in the labour force. The employment equity Bill requires that annual reports be filed. Has the Hon. Member looked at what effect that has had on women in the workforce who will be threatened because of the readjustment program which will be necessary if this dreadful trade Bill ever gets implemented? Is there an ability, by passing legislation with clout, to protect these women? What kind of adjustment programs would the Hon. Member be suggesting?

Mr. Speaker, I think this is the kernel of the problem. I mentioned earlier a level playing field and what will constitute an unfair subsidy. This is one of the problems with the whole trade deal.
In terms of programs which may assist women who are dislocated through this deal or through other measures, there are a number of things that could be done. Certainly there could be programs to assist older workers. Older women contribute much to our economy.
As I mentioned earlier, the Canadian Jobs Strategy has glaring gaps. In study after study, there has been identified one of the basic needs which is for literacy programs and upgrading programs for both men and women. Again, we are simply seeing more money going to the private sector and less money going to the colleges that do this kind of work. This is a very severe crisis.
I have spoken with many people in my constituency and in others about funding for literacy programs, for example, and that level of funding is abysmal. Yet we do not seem to want to come to grips with the fact that a very large percentage of our citizens are not literate.
There are many programs that could be put into place to assist women in getting training. Some of the CEIC programs are very restrictive in terms of the allowances given for child care. We keep coming back to child care. I am sorry to say that we have to keep coming back to it.
I was speaking about aboriginal women earlier. Child care is an extremely serious issue on reserves. Many women who want to work simply cannot. In fact, many native women to whom I have spoken in my constituency simply cannot work because there is no child care available. Similarly, if they wish to obtain training they cannot because there is no child care

available. We keep returning to that issue, and that will certainly be a very major factor.
Child care is not a woman's program, it is a family program. However, it will certainly help those women who are dislocated, either through simple changes in industry or through the trade deal, and those women who wish to upgrade their skills so that they can be more competitive in the market-place.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to rise in this House in support of the effort to provide more equality, freedom and opportunities for women. I would like to thank my colleague of the New Democratic Party for having moved this motion.
I believe that the Conservative Government has made some effort to help women achieve equality. However, there is still a lot of room for improvement. We only have to look at child care, employment equity and programs for women in nontraditional sectors. I think that the Government should do more in these areas.
First, however, I would like to deal with what women do now and how they live today. I know that the Canadian family has changed a lot and that 60 per cent of couples with children work full-time because they need two salaries to raise their children properly.
Naturally, the majority of women today try to combine their heavy workload at home with their job in the labour force, and as everyone knows, the cost of raising children is increasing. From the moment a child starts to go to school until the age of 18, he will cost $106,000. In addition, a couple with children must earn $6,000 more a year to have the same way of life as a childless couple. Moreoever, child care costs between $4,000 and $8,000 a year per child.
If we look at single-parent families, we wonder how they can possibly afford these services. We must not forget, as was mentioned by a number of our colleagues, that 72 per cent of single-parent families are headed by women, and that half of that 72 per cent lives on less than $10,000 a year. These are recent statistics, and the figures are not for 1981 but for 198586.
These figures should come as no surprise, when we consider that the majority of part-time workers are women, and that these women do not get maternity leave, annual leave or sick leave.
These are things most people take for granted. The unemployment rate is considerably higher for women than it is for men. Women's salaries are still only 60 per cent of men's salaries. Women make up 82 per cent of the labour force in low-paying clerical jobs, and 63 per cent of the unskilled manufacturing jobs.

Mr. Speaker, these figures tell us that the role of women and the role of the family has changed. Although women have more choices than they had before, they still have a long way to go, and we should not forget that the majority of women are relegated to employment ghettos, in other words, to low-paying jobs.
Is it so surprising that one million children in Canada live in poverty? Is it so surprising that our birth rate is only 1.7? Is it so surprising that parents decide to have fewer children? They cannot afford more, and our society does not provide them with the support services they need to raise happy, healthy children.
As a society, we claim to believe in equality. We support the principle that women must have the same opportunities as men. How can we expect to achieve equality if we do not help women to carry the heavy domestic burden that is traditionally theirs?
What will ever become of Canadian families if we continue to expect each working woman to be a superwoman, busy with a full-time career and all the while raising her children? Pious wishes are simply not good enough, Mr. Speaker, action is what we need.

One of the things the federal Government has done is to allocate $5.4 billion to a new national strategy for child care. This sounds very impressive, but if we look closely at the program we see that the Conservative Government has actually cheated the less-privileged children in Canada. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised affordable, quality child care for all Canadian children, but on December 3, 1987, he broke that promise.
The government program allocated $3 billion of the $5.4 billion to federal-provincial cost-sharing programs, with the objective of creating 200,000 new day care spaces.
[ Translation]
We have a problem here, Mr. Speaker: only 10 per cent of all children aged 13 or under have access to child care programs. Over a million children are looking for day care space, yet at this time the Government can respond to only 25 per cent of all applications.
We know that over the past five years day care spaces have increased by 19 per cent; now if that rate were to be maintained during the next seven years, and without assistance under the program established by the Conservative Government, we would end up with more than 900,000 spaces in 1995, but instead we will have only 400,000. Thence the impression that the Conservative Government limits instead of speeding up the creation of day care spaces.

The Liberal Party has been demanding a national child care program for a long time. The Government did a good job of
March 9, 1988

avoiding the issue for a long time. The Liberal Party demanded and is still demanding immediate funds to meet the immediate crisis of a lack of child care spaces, but we do not know when we are going to see those new spaces created. The Government will hand out money for space creation only when it has negotiated with the provinces. When will these negotiations be completed? Next month? Next year? Two years from now? What will Canadian children do in the meantime?

It will also be very important for the federal Government to set a goal in terms of the percentage of spaces it would like to fund through the CAP because, depending on the wealth of each province, the Government could provide support and ensure access to low and medium income families.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party also proposes both the establisment of a program of quality and the provision of funds that would also be paid for staffing those child care centres. But right now there is very little spaces being created and very little money paid to ensure quality, because the Government set no standards and established no supervision program as to how the money will be used, how it will be spent and what types of child care services will be created in the various provinces.
There is a danger of course of having service disparities based on the direction taken by each province, and we could wake up with child care services that would be operated on the same basis as senior citizen homes, namely that if you have money you will have good services for your children in those child care centres-if parents have the money-and if you have less money there would be lower quality services. I do not think Canada is on the verge of collapse to the point of not being more open to child care. People always state child care centres are a priority, more money is needed. But those who want to operate a parking lot can more easily get bank loans than people who want to open child care centres, because let us not forget, people who want to open child care centres cannot get bank loans!
In fact, they will be told that this is not a business, it is not taken seriously. On the other hand, you can obtain a bank loan for any small concern that you want to set up. However, daycare centres are not considered a business. As far as I can remember, the federal Government has not responded to one of the recommendations made in the report suggesting that people who would like to open day care centres at home or elsewhere be entitled to bank loans.
In addition, when we consider the cost of day care centres, we realize that a child can cost from $4,000 to $8,000 per year. Of course, at present most families cannot afford such services. The cost of those services should be divided among federal and provincial governments, employers and parents. And the parents should not pay more than a pro rata of their earnings or half of the fees at day care centres, especially the average family.
Supply
And of course, there is the famous CAP which should be open and made available to low and average income families. We are still waiting for it. The Government says that it has taken steps, but once again, we would like to speed them up. Unfortunately, the Tory government did not hear our pleas. Instead of creating more spaces, it provides $2.3 billion for new income tax deductions. This means that those who can afford to pay $5,000 per year for the care of their children can obtain a $4,000 deduction. However, those who cannot pay that amount, will receive absolutely nothing.
Canadian women need immediate funds from the Government to create new child care spaces now. Every province should be adhering to nationally set standards of quality and affordability. We need money put into programs for latchkey children, for longer parental leave at birth, for day care at night and for quality day care training, not for regressive tax deductions. This is an issue of extreme importance for Canadian women and the present Government has bypassed it.

In this Tory Government's response to the majority report, there is no mention of parental leaves. Recommendations have been made to the Government because we feel that if we want couples to have more children, we must provide them with support services. In addition to day care services, we must provide them with parental leave.
The majority report on day care services was not the only report which had made recommendations to this effect, Mr. Speaker. The Forget Report and the equality report had asked for an extension of up to 26 weeks of parental leave. There is no mention of this in the Government's response. There is no mention either of what will happen to the "latchkey children". We know that 54 per cent of all children between the ages of 6 and 13 are alone at home when they return from school. Of course, the Government is quite silent concerning the recommendations we had made in this report.
In the United States, according to a recently published study which appeared yesterday in the media, an increasing number of children between the ages of 6 and 13 find refuge in libraries. In fact, the Governments of several states have introduced legislation to make it illegal for parents to leave their children in libraries after school. It is because the need for day care services has not been met there, and I would not want a similar situation to occur in Canada. Several parents came forward with a request to see to it that parents may have access to school premises once school is over. We know that the province of Quebec is the only province where school principals are authorized to keep school premises open for parents who want to organize supervision committes to keep an eye on their children until 6 p.m. or 7 p.m.
A number of recommendations have been made to that end-we know that this is a provincial responsibility-and

March 9, 1988
Supply
when the time comes for the federal Government to meet its Provincial counterparts to discuss the CAP program, it might show leadership and ask provincial Governments, especially through their Ministers of Education, to act with extreme diligence in this matter to take care of these children. It would certainly be far less expensive for the federal Government and the provincial Governments to provide day care for children than to pay delinquency costs. We know that a deliquent child costs us $44,000 a year. Children who are in foster homes cost a lot of money to the Government, but if we had a prevention policy, we could plan and it would be less expensive and our children would be far better off.
Furthermore, the Government committed itself to the promotion of job equality for women and to their participation in the job-entry programs in non traditional sectors. I think that my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) demonstrated very well that the Conservative Government has been dragging its feet in this area and that it has not yet kept all its promises. I would also like to mention-

The Conservative Government has cut spending on job training by 23 per cent since 1985. Under the Canadian Jobs Strategy program funds were shifted from the public to the private sector for on the job training. It has been found that employers have favoured men over women for training. There are no controls in place to monitor employers or to evaluate the work skills acquired by training.
Also, there is almost no funding in language training to help female immigrants. The Government seems to assume that female immigrants will be provided for by their spouses or will take jobs that do not require language skills. As a result, many find themselves doing menial labour with no benefits and no way out.
Some programs under the Canadian Jobs Strategy are targeted at women. To be eligible for most of these programs women must be unemployed anywhere from eight months to three years. Any woman who cannot afford to stay out of work that long cannot profit from these training programs.
Training allowances are still less than minimum wage. How can a woman who supports a family afford to get job training if the Government gives her no financial aid? Unless the training programs change and unless the Government allocates more funds soon, many women will have little hope of bettering their economic prospect.

There is still looming on the horizon the free trade agreement. We have heard women and we know that for several months now they have been voicing their concern about that agreement because it will affect the service sector in which most of them work. We ask the Government to move quickly, to establish programs that will help women adjust to the new conditions. I just want to say that I recognize the Liberal
Government had made room for women and I wish the Conservative Government would follow in its steps. I think the Liberal Government showed the direction in which I would like to see the Conservative Government go. I agree of course with the Minister responsible for the Status of Women and I know she cares very much about the condition of women in Canada, but I would like her party to be as concerned as she is and act with greater vigour and leadership.

Mr. Speaker, in her remarks, the Hon. Member referred to what is occurring in the United States where parents, mothers, leave their children in libraries. I wonder whether she could provide more information about that.

Mr. Speaker, there have been reports published about libraries being the favorite places for kids to gather after school. Having no place else to go after school hours, and with parents still at work, kids are invading every public library.
Confronted with that situation, library managers have complained that their premises were no child care centre. And parents were thus requested to look after their children. With the result now that several states just passed legislation providing that parents will be charged with gross negligence if their children, between 6 and 13 years of age, are found in a public library after school. Those parents will have to arrange to have their children looked after elsewhere.
That worries me because it shows there is a problem, not only here, in Canada, where 54 per cent of our children are concerned, but also in the United States, and, as the saying goes, when the United States has a cold, Canada catches pneumonia six months later! I would not like the same to happen here. I believe it is still time to remedy the situation in Canada, providing the Government establishes a program and makes recommendations regarding "latchkey children" because, right now, some have nowhere to turn. It could, as I mentioned earlier, co-operate with provincial Governments and the Ministers of Education. The latter could decide to open their schools to these children. Surely, parents would agree to sharing the cost of paying a salary to those who would supervise their children after school hours.
Unfortunately, however, I am somewhat concerned since the Government did not respond at all to the recommendations contained in the majority report.
Thus the Government must act diligently on this issue, and without any delay.

Mr. Speaker, I am a little puzzled by this statement about children being left in libraries in the U.S. In her comments, the Hon. Member seemed to say that they were of course left by themselves without any supervision.
Could the Hon. Member gives us more details? What did these children do during the long hours they were left alone? Were they going around looking at books? I understand the librarians did not like it very much.
March 9, 1988

I was also wondering about the children's age. She said they were from 10 to 12 years old, but were there among them any children under six left without any supervision?
Of course, that would make the example more concrete and understandable. If there were three or four-year olds left by themselves, then it would reinforce the example just mentioned by the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, the report was referring to school children from first grade up. Those children range in age from 5 to 12. They invade libraries where they take up space, and adults cannot read in peace. You know what six-year-old children are like, how they whisper and so on-all peace and quiet was gone. Above all, librarians said that their job was to serve customers and not to keep an eye on children running everywhere. They can be allowed to read a book but... The library was turning into a day care centre!
However, I was told that in Montreal and some other big cities Canadian parents are already using the same strategy. They say, "We are going to leave our child at the library because it is safe." They tell the child, "Wait for mommy or daddy to come and pick you up at such and such a time." Then, after school, the child goes to the library, sits down and reads. If there is only one or two, they will be quiet. But if you have 10 or so children of the same age, they are very difficult to control and it is no longer a library. Adults were also quite disturbed and said: "It is impossible for us to come and read peacefully because at those hours, children invade the libraries."
What worries me, is the fact that the Government adopted a very strict law accusing parents of gross negligence with their children. But on the other side, parents need only a service to help them with their children. I don't want the same kind of situation here. Usually, we don't do anything for those children. During the committee hearings on child care, parents from all over Canada asked us the same thing: "Please, do something for our children!" It would be socially less costly to act. Some say that there are too many delinquents, that our children are depressed, that teenagers commit suicide, and it has always been our conviction that if we could provide good child care services to low income families with low education, those children would graduate from high school, probably go to college and would be in a position to find a job instead of becoming members of a third generation of welfare recipients because nobody ever took care of them.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to join in the debate this afternoon on the motion of the Hon. Member for Hamilton (Ms. Dewar). To begin with, I must say that I do not agree with her motion. In fact, I would say the situation is quite the opposite. Since this Government came to office in September, 1984, we have deliberately and intentionally taken initiatives and advanced
Supply
policies which clearly demonstrate our support for the aspirations of Canadian women.
We have also attacked the sources of discrimination. It sometimes seems as though opposition Members want to turn a blind eye to all of these accomplishments and a deaf ear to our achievements in fostering equality for women. As the Hon. Minister has already indicated, and as I have myself, we are particularly proud of our achievements with respect to the opportunities for women in the labour force. We look over the past three and a half years and we see over 1.1 million jobs created, the majority of those jobs being for women. We have seen an increasing number of women coming into the workforce. In fact, the recent Statistics Canada report indicates some very major changes which are taking place in our society. It shows that the women's labour force participation rate has increased from 51.8 per cent, to 55.9 per cent and that the highest participation rate is for married women living with a spouse whose children are under the age of six. In fact, that rate has increased from 49.5 per cent in 1981 to 62.1 per cent in 1986. Obviously, the majority are women in their twenties and early thirties. They may have taken a break for a period of time when bearing their children, but they are now going back to work and pursuing a career or job for a variety of reasons. It could be for their own sense of self-fulfilment and in other circumstances it could be economically necessary. I do not think the reason matters. We are seeing some major changes taking place in Canadian society.
I wanted to focus my remarks today on a very important strategy of the Government which, I think, appropriately reflects this change in the workforce, particularly the fact that so many women with children under the age of six are maintaining their role in the workforce. That, of course, is the issue of child care and the recognition of its importance with the introduction of the national strategy on child care as a case in point.
We have heard that there are about 250,000 child care spaces in Canada. These spaces are all that exist to serve the needs of working women, women who seek to improve themselves through education and training. One might conclude from the recent report of Statistics Canada that a quarter of a million spaces is obviously not enough to provide the child care services required for working mothers. I remind the House that this situation did not arise suddenly and without warning. It was allowed to develop over a succession of Governments. This Government sought election on the promise of the expansion of child care services in Canada. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has delivered on this promise with his presentation of the National Strategy on Child Care.
It is both unreasonable and unfair to assert, as does the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain, that the Government has failed to address discrimination against Canadian women. Indeed, the national strategy is clear and irrefutable evidence that this Government is deliberate in its support of the rights

Supply
and aspirations of women to participate as equals in the Canadian workforce.
Let us consider Canadian mothers who, because of income or circumstances, cannot afford the necessary child care to free them to take a job or to seek education. Over the past 15 years federal Governments have shared, through the Canada Assistance Plan, provincial development of child care systems. As we all know, the delivery of this service is within the jurisdiction of the provinces. To date this has resulted in the creation of 140,000 subsidized child care spaces across the country. We know that this number of spaces is not sufficient to meet the needs of lower income working women or single mothers who need child care to allow them to take the training which would give them access to the workforce. The Government did not, like others before it, simply pay lip-service to the need for more subsidized child care spaces. Nor was it satisfied to see an unsystematic increase in spaces. Rather, within the national strategy, it intentionally set a goal for the creation of new subsidized spaces.
Within the next seven years we will see the creation of some
200,000	new subsidized spaces. Within seven years there will be almost three times the number of currently subsidized spaces. Within the next seven years there will be created almost twice the number of subsidized spaces created over the past 15 years. I think that record of progress and its acceleration is very dramatic.
Surely any fair and reasonable person would accept the Government's commitment to the creation of this number of subsidized child care spaces as evidence of sensitivity to the needs of those women who have the greatest child care needs because those are the women at whom this program is directed. It is directed at those women in the lower income areas who need access to subsidized child care. It is also evidence of concern that the lack of affordable child care is a barrier to women assuming an equitable place in the workforce and a commitment to reduce discrimination against women.
In short, it is self-evident that the national strategy on child care is predicated upon addressing a fundamental basis of discrimination against women. As mothers we are the primary care givers to children. Yet our choices are often fewer because our priority will always be with our children. In the interests of our children it is sometimes necessary to either sacrifice or to reduce our career aspirations. When we do venture into the workforce we have had sometimes to settle for jobs that are lower paying, below our capabilities and sometimes not particularly challenging because we are having to balance the issue of addressing our responsibilities to our families with trying to maintain a job.
However, in other circumstances, there really is not even a choice for the single woman, for the woman in a low income household. They really have to venture into the workforce to provide a semblance of economic stability for themselves and
their children. However, often they are very vulnerable to discrimination. Thus working mothers without access to child care are, by definition, the victims of discrimination.
The longer Canada's child care policy and system was allowed to unfold as it might without any set goals, the longer such discrimination continued. It was this Government which recognized the simple fact and intervened deliberately to see that more child care spaces would become available to working women and that more of these spaces would be affordable and thus accessible to women who need them most. That is an important differentiation to make.
When I hear members of other Parties suggest that child care should be universally available or free I do not think the majority of Canadians feel that way. I think the majority of Canadians feel that it is important to have high quality child care services available and that for those women who need the assistance there should be appropriate subsidies available for them.
It is a very familiar complaint, particularly of young parents, that the bulk of the incomes of working mothers goes to pay their child care costs. While working mothers may be satisfying career aspirations, they are not left with enough take-home pay to make much of a difference in the quality of their family lives. Child care has become an onerous cost of employment for women. That, too, is a form of discrimination.
Thus, as we saw with the national strategy on child care within the recent Budget, the Government recognized that the burden of child care costs was discriminatory. We have taken steps to reduce that burden through changes to the tax system as it applies to child care. The child care expense deduction has been doubled from $2,000 to $4,000 per annum for each child six years and younger and for children with special care needs beyond that age. As a result, parents will be able to deduct more of their real child care costs when calculating their income tax. The working woman will be able to have more of her income in hand. Even though my children are well beyond those ages I know, from looking back at the time when they were small and I was working, that that certainly would have been a very welcome initiative. In those days my income was not very great. This is something which will help women from all sectors in coping with the increasing costs of child care.
Young and growing families will benefit from the removal of the $8,000 ceiling on their child care expense deduction. Parents are now allowed to deduct $4,000 of child care receipts for each of their children six years and under, and $2,000 for children age seven to fourteen years regardless of the total of these deductions. Thus for larger families child care has become more affordable. We are no longer discriminating against larger families. It seems to me that the policies that were in place before were unfair and inappropriate to larger families.
There are many Canadian families which make use of informal child care, the baby-sitting type arrangement. They
March 9, 1988

do not receive receipts for the costs of the care. Under the tax deduction for income tax one has to have these receipts. This is to ensure that people are not trying to fool the system. Elowever, this measure will allow more flexibility for families to choose traditional day care arrangements, to have someone come into the home or to have other arrangements. I believe that Canadian families want that kind of flexibility. They do not want one limited kind of system. Those who are not taking advantage of this, such as lower income parents, will benefit from the new $200 supplement to the child tax credit. Beginning this year, 1988, such parents will receive a supplement of $100 in respect of children six years and younger. They will receive an additional $100 next year.
These supplements will increase the child tax credit from about $535 to $760 per child in 1989. That is really quite a significant amount of money, particularly for lower income families. The effect of these changes in the tax system is to make child care more affordable to Canadian families. They reduce the burden of child care as an expense in employment for the working mother. They address a source of discrimination against tens if not hundreds of thousands of women. Once again, any fair or reasonable person would not see in this initiative a failure to address discrimination against Canadian women. Indeed, any fair and reasonable person would see in this initiative an attempt to ensure for women increasing equity in their disposable incomes.
Sometimes discrimination is a matter of locality or geography. Because Canada is such a large country this sometimes happens. No one would deny that farm women are partners in operating Canada's farms. They work as hard and as long as any woman who has a career in business, industry or the professions. However, they do not usually have access to care for their children. Canada's child care system has not expanded into most of rural Canada. Similarly, young families in the northern reaches of our provinces and in our two northern territories generally do not have access to child care.
As part of the national child care strategy there is the new child care initiatives fund. It will support innovative demonstration, development and applied research projects to child care. It will look at opportunities to provide child care in rural and under-serviced areas to provide for the needs of women going into special training programs. I hope it will also look at the needs of young women in the school system. In Ottawa, Rideau High School has established an informal child care program, and they are talking about expanding it. This will support the teenage woman who wants to go back to high school. She would have the child care facilities right there in school. That would be a big encouragement for those young women to be able to return to school and complete their education, and ultimately become economically self-sufficient. That seems to me one way of not only reducing discrimination, but of creating real opportunities and choices for the women of this
Supply
country. Surely, that is the goal of all of us on all sides of this House.
As the country proceeds to expand the availability of child care spaces, there will be a continued demand for qualified child care workers. The expansion of Canadian child care services will create 40,000 new jobs across this land. Under the Canadian Jobs Strategy program the Government has supported and will continue to support the training of new child care workers, most of whom will probably be new entrants into the workforce.
Even this very cursory examination of the national strategy on child care would lead any fair and reasonable person to conclude that we are indeed preoccupied with the equity of women as participants in Canadian society, with the economic equality of Canadian women, and with equality of opportunity for women. The national strategy is not an element of discrimination, and does not fail to address discrimination against women. Rather, it is a full-blown attack upon a major source of discrimination.
The Government is providing, in partnership with the provinces, territories, and parents, a tremendous boost to the expansion of child care services. We have allocated $5.4 billion over the next seven years to support that expansion. That breaks down to federal Government cost sharing expenditures of $3 billion, tax measures of $2.3 billion, and the special initiatives fund of $100 million. It lays the ground work for a new social utility in this country to support the aspiring and working women of Canada.
In looking in more detail at only the federal-provincial cost sharing aspect, I would ask you to consider this fact, Mr. Speaker. In the 15 years that the federal Government has been cost sharing child care with the provinces under the Canada Assistance Plan, the Government has spent approximately $1.5 billion as its share of the cost. However, within the new national strategy, the Government proposes within only the federal-provincial cost sharing arrangement to spend $3 billion over the next seven years. In other words, the Government will spend twice the amount of money in half the amount of time on cost sharing federal-provincial programs for child care.
If this magnitude of commitment to child care is judged by the Hon. Member to represent failure, then one is hard pressed to characterize the performance of previous Governments. No, Mr. Speaker, this Government has not failed Canadian women. It has decreased sources of discrimination, it is empowering women to participate more fully, and it is promoting their economic equality. Any fair and reasonable review of the national strategy on child care would conclude that this is so, and not only in the field of child care, but in employment and in all the policies of this Government. Canadian women can look forward to increased economic opportunities and increased opportunities for social justice.
